title: When Diagnosis Curls a Little: Partial Bowel Obstruction Due to Ascaris. L in a Young Man
case_text:
A 19-year-old man presented to the ER with abdominal pain and constipation for three weeks. The pain was gradual and progressive, scoring six out of 10. Nausea and vomiting (which happened only once and was not bilious) developed 48 h before his ER visit. Previously, he was in good health and had no relevant medical history like abdominal surgery. He had a heart rate of 87 beats per minute, blood pressure of 110/70 mm Hg, and normal respiratory rate. Upon examination, the abdomen was without distention and surgical scar. It was also soft without tenderness. No mass was palpable in superficial or deep palpation. The rectal exam was empty. Lab studies showed a hemoglobin level of 14 g per deciliter (reference range, 12-15 g/dl) and a white blood cell level of 7600 per cubic millimeter (reference range, 4000 to 11,000 WBC/muL). On detailed history, he remembered that he had passed some worms on his last defecation.
A stool exam for eggs and parasites revealed fertilized eggs from roundworms of the species Ascaris lumbricoides, and a diagnosis of ascariasis was established. Abdominopelvic CT with oral contrast was performed, and it (Figs. 1 and 2) revealed worm-like masses as longitudinal filling defects in the ileum. Partial bowel obstruction was treated with conservative management, and then the patient was treated with mebendazole and was referred to an infectious disease specialist for further treatment.
The patient was an Afghan immigrant to Iran who immigrated over a year ago and worked as a construction worker. Because of the low socioeconomic level, he does not have environmental sanitation and personal hygiene. In extended history, the patient recalled drinking from a water source with inadequate hygiene, which can be the source of Ascaris transmission. It was recommended that the patient be more cautious about the sanitaryness of food and water. He lives alone, but prophylaxis treatment is crucial if infected patients live with roommates.

Your job is to transform a published clinical case report into a standardized admission diagnostic teaching case following the Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology.

RULES (Read Carefully — No Exceptions):
1. SOURCE FIDELITY:
   - Extract facts ONLY from the supplied case report.
   - Do NOT invent, embellish, or smooth out missing clinical data.
   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Soil-Transmitted Helminths
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: ascariasis with partial bowel obstruction
